newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton to boost Asia ties on Australia visit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to boost Asia ties on Australia visit.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton arrived in Australia on Tuesday at the start of his first overseas trip since his re-election, signalling the continuing importance of Asia during his second term in office.
Accompanied by his wife, Hillary, Clinton flew into Sydney on Air Force One to a stately 21-gun salute and a red-carpet welcome from Prime Minister John Howard.

On a breezy spring evening, the Clintons were also greeted by Governor-General William Deane, the representative of Australia's head-of-state, Queen Elizabeth, before stopping off to greet a crowd of around 150 well-wishers.
On Wednesday, on his first full day in Australia, Clinton is to visit the capital of Canberra for talks with Howard and to address a joint sitting of both houses of parliament.
A senior U.S. official said on Tuesday that Clinton would use that speech to highlight the historically close relations between Australia and the United States.
But he will also prepare the ground for what is seen as the main event of his nine-day Asia-Pacific trip -- a meeting with Chinese President Jiang Zemin in Manila on Sunday.

U.S. officials have said that Clinton was eager to make the United States' role in the Asia-Pacific region a foreign policy priority during his second term in office and point out his first trip after winning the election in 1992 was also to Asia.
The official said Clinton would call for a deeper engagement with China, hoping to improve relations perennially dogged by rows over human rights and trade.
It is a message that should go down well in Australia and especially with Howard's conservative coalition government, which came to power in March.

Howard has tried to boost Canberra's ties with the United States, which he says were neglected under his predecessor, Paul Keating, who pushed forward his desire for Australia to embrace Asia and improve its standing in the fast-growing region.

But Howard's strategic move to boost ties with Washington, combined with a series of diplomatic spats between Canberra and Beijing, appears to have upset China, which has accused Australia of being a pawn in an unstated U.S. policy of containment.

"We value the fact that China invests more in Australia than any other country," Howard said in a newspaper interview on Tuesday. "We want a good relationship...I certainly don't want to see China isolated."
After his visit to Canberra, where he will also lay a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, Clinton will return to Sydney for an evening cruise on the harbour hosted by Howard.
Then begin three days dominated by leisure when the Clintons will enjoy Australia's natural beauty and put the rigours of election campaigning behind them.

Apart from a speech to the Australian people from a site near the Sydney Opera House on Thursday, Clinton's schedule is largely free -- allowing him time for at least one game of golf. Australia's world number one Greg Norman and rising U.S. star Tiger Woods, both playing in a Sydney tournament, are potential partners.
On Thursday evening, the Clintons fly off to the tropical resort of Port Douglas on the Great Barrier Reef for two days of swimming, snorkelling and, probably, more golf.
The president and his entourage leave Sydney on Saturday for the Philippines, where he will join the annual leaders' summit of the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum on Monday.
